children: By Jodi Xu Klein, Andrew Scurria and Alexander Gladstone
A couple of Weil Gotshal & Manges restructuring partners are set to join onetime rival Sullivan & Cromwell as the storied law firm winds down, according to people familiar with the matter.

Restructuring partners Ronit Berkovich and Gary Holtzer are headed for Sullivan & Cromwell, those people said. Meanwhile, Matt Barr, global chair of Weil's restructuring practice, is in talks to join Skadden along with partners Sunny Singh and Jeff Saferstein, they said.
Representatives for Weil, Sullivan & Cromwell, and Skadden didn't immediately respond to requests seeking comment.

Weil's swift collapse has left hundreds of lawyers and staff rushing to find other jobs. Weil's partners this week voted to wind down the firm after it announced its intention internally in late October.

Weil's restructuring practice, which employed more than 140 attorneys and was the crown jewel of the firm, had in recent years lost ground to rivals such as Kirkland & Ellis and Latham & Watkins, which aggressively expanded their offerings through lateral hires.

Other firms have been courting members of Weil's restructuring practice as well, including Cleary Gottlieb and Paul Weiss, people familiar with the matter said. Representatives for Cleary and Paul Weiss didn't immediately comment.

Weil's restructuring practice took off in the late 1980s after Congress overhauled the bankruptcy code to give companies more flexibility to restructure their debt. The group, under the leadership of Harvey Miller, gained stature and showed how the law can be used to address a range of corporate issues. The team guided restructurings for notable cases, including Enron, WorldCom, American Airlines and Lehman Brothers in the following years.

Its dominance began to chip away in the following decade, after Miller's death in 2015, as rivals continued expanding their practices. The rise of liability management exercises later ushered restructuring into a new era driven by private-equity-owned companies. Weil fell out of the top 10 for company-side representations in the first nine months of this year. Its sudden collapse leaves the already tightly-knit restructuring market with even fewer major players.
